updated_reason: The read holds from Nov. 18. Manfred said owners will not compromise on a cap and floor, and the union answered with a public jab over revenue-share math rather than a counterproposal. With no sessions scheduled and both sides dug in on the core system, the odds still tilt toward a stoppage that reaches the regular season.
summary: Both sides have already moved toward each other on free agency, the qualifying offer and the minimum salary. The fight is over the system itself: owners say a cap and floor is non-negotiable, and players say any cap is a non-starter. A deal most likely needs a structure that gives owners spending limits in practice without the word cap.
common_ground: Scrap the qualifying offer (both sides have proposed it)
Free agency after five years of service for players 30 and older (both sides)
A higher minimum salary (MLB offers $900K to $1M, the union wants $1.5M)
More revenue sharing between clubs (both sides, in different forms)
Progress reported on non-economic items such as grievances, drug policy and gambling rules
Interest in MLB players at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics

middle_ground.title: A floor and a steep tax instead of a hard cap
middle_ground.how: Keep a payroll floor, but replace the hard cap with a much steeper luxury tax above a high threshold, with draft-pick and roster penalties for repeat offenders.
middle_ground.owners_get: A real spending band: low payrolls rise and top payrolls face penalties strong enough to act like a ceiling.
middle_ground.players_get: No hard limit on salaries, so a team can still pay its stars if it accepts the tax.
middle_ground.precedent: The NBA's soft cap with tax aprons, which the 2011 NBA lockout settled on after 161 days.

middle_ground.title: Spend what you are shared
middle_ground.how: Expand revenue sharing as both sides want, but require clubs that receive it to meet a minimum payroll each year.
middle_ground.owners_get: More money moved from big markets to small ones, which they proposed.
middle_ground.players_get: Guaranteed spending by low-payroll teams, which addresses their long-standing complaint about clubs pocketing shared revenue.
middle_ground.precedent: Spending floors tied to shared revenue in the NFL and NBA systems.

middle_ground.title: A guaranteed share band instead of a 50-50 split
middle_ground.how: Guarantee players a share of league revenue within a band, settled with a year-end true-up, without capping individual team payrolls.
middle_ground.owners_get: Cost certainty at the league level, the main goal behind the 50-50 proposal.
middle_ground.players_get: Protection of their current share, which the union puts at 55 to 56 percent and Manfred puts below 50.
middle_ground.precedent: The NBA's revenue-based escrow and true-up system.

middle_ground.title: Phase it in and test it
middle_ground.how: Build on MLB's move to delay any cap until 2028: adopt the floor now, and trigger stronger spending limits later only if agreed competitive-balance measures are missed, with an opt-out after three seasons.
middle_ground.owners_get: A path to the system they want on the books.
middle_ground.players_get: Time, an off-ramp, and limits that only apply if balance actually worsens.
middle_ground.precedent: Mid-term opt-outs in recent NBA and NHL agreements.

middle_ground.title: Trade spending limits for young-player pay
middle_ground.how: Pair any new spending limits with the union's top asks: a minimum salary near $1.5M, a bigger pre-arbitration bonus pool and earlier free agency.
middle_ground.owners_get: Their structural change, paid for mostly by spending at the bottom of the roster.
middle_ground.players_get: Raises for the majority of players who earn near the minimum.
middle_ground.precedent: The 2022 MLB deal, which ended a 99-day lockout with a higher minimum and a new pre-arbitration bonus pool.

scenarios.name: Quick deal
scenarios.season_impact: Normal spring training and a full season
scenarios.how_it_ends: Owners set the hard cap aside for a floor plus a much steeper luxury tax, and the union accepts a floor in exchange for a big minimum-salary raise and the free agency changes both sides already back.
signals: Either side drops cap or no-cap language from public statements
Owners stop describing the cap and floor as non-negotiable

scenarios.name: Spring deal, short delay
scenarios.season_impact: Shortened spring training; Opening Day may slip a week or two, with games likely made up as in 2022
scenarios.how_it_ends: Pressure builds as spring training is canceled. The sides settle on a soft-cap system: a payroll floor, a high tax threshold with steep penalties that limit spending in practice, and a guaranteed band for the players' share of revenue.
signals: MLB postpones spring training games without canceling regular-season dates
Talk of a soft cap or tax aprons in reporting

scenarios.name: Games lost
scenarios.season_impact: Regular-season games canceled, likely a season of roughly 100 to 120 games
scenarios.how_it_ends: Neither side moves until losses mount and the 60-game point that would extend national TV deals approaches. Either players accept a cap with a high ceiling, a solid floor and large gains elsewhere, as NHL players did after losing 2004-05, or owners settle for a floor and stiff tax after legal pressure such as a union disclaimer of interest.
signals: The union disclaims interest or files antitrust claims
Owner unity cracks, or players publicly split on a cap

method: Our editorial read of the reporting, revised with each update. Odds are judgment, not a forecast model or betting line. Middle-ground options are drawn from each side's reported proposals and from how other leagues and past MLB labor fights were settled.
